$comment: Golden vectors for WHERE a side's data lives, and what a person is told about it.
Both halves derive this independently — `PanelSettings.ResolveDataDir` / `StorageNotes` in C#
(src_mcp/src/Server/PanelSettings.cs) and `dataDir.ts` in the extension — because the extension
WRITES the Team-server token under this directory and the MCP shim READS it, and because the
panel now tells a person which directory this window resolved. A divergence is therefore two
different failures at once: a sign-in that silently is not there, and a panel giving migration
advice that contradicts the server's own startup log.
Isolated unit tests on each side cannot catch that, because each side is self-consistent. Only a
shared fixture can, which is why this file sits outside both and is asserted by both suites.
Raised by codex and gemini independently on the plan round of the panel half (2026-09-14).
`dir` is the resolved directory with `<root>` standing for the absolute form of `COAI_DATA_DIR`,
because the two languages spell an absolute path differently on one platform and identically on
the other. `refused` means the side was asked for and cannot be used: the server refuses to
start and the panel renders the refusal rather than guessing a path.
`notes` names which of the two sentences applies, not their wording — the wording is each side's
own and is allowed to read naturally in its own surface. What must not differ is WHETHER a
person is warned.
- `loose-database`: a coai.db sits directly in the shared root while this side resolves
elsewhere. It is not being used; move it into a side directory to keep its history.
- `new-directory`:  the resolved directory does not exist yet, so this side starts with no
history. A typo in COAI_DATA_DIR looks exactly like this.

vectors.why: nothing configured — the default, which this change must not move
a chosen directory and no side — used exactly as chosen, as it always was
the operator's own case: two installations, one NAS, a side each
a side name is lower-cased, so the two halves agree on case as well as on shape
the history left behind by the flat layout — reported, never adopted
a mistyped NAS path is a creatable directory, and looks exactly like a fresh side
both at once: old history in the root, and this side has never run
a plausible thing to type, and the one that must never fall back to the shared root
a colon is refused on Windows and accepted on Linux, so the grammar refuses it everywhere
dot and dot-dot are directory names no side may claim
a space is not in the grammar either — one rule, simple enough to write twice
